**Solution 1 (3n+1) is wrong.** Its host is K₁ + nP₃, with v adjacent to every vertex. The adversary puts {v, a₁, b₁} in one red clique. Then c₁ has no blue neighbour among the remaining vertices, so the blue centre v has only n−1 usable blue pairs. The proof's "compensating pair" step is hand-waved and fails here.

**Solution 3 (2n+2) is wrong.** Its lower-bound colouring is not valid. It makes cv₁ and cw₁ red but leaves v₁w₁ blue, so v₁–c–w₁ is an induced red K₁,₂. The condition is that the red neighbourhood must be a red clique, not merely an F-clique. Its upper-bound argument is also only a sketch.

**Solution 2 (3n+4) has a valid construction.** Take F = K₁ + (n+1)P₃. Any red-class structure must be a clique partition, and cliques lie inside single P₃'s. If the centre c is a singleton, each of the n+1 paths contributes a blue edge, and edges from different paths are non-adjacent, giving a blue induced F_n. If c shares a class with one path's two vertices, the other n full paths still give an induced matching of size n. So 3n+4 is an upper bound.

I could not fully verify the lower bound. Ruling out all hosts on 3n+3 vertices needs a complete argument, and Solution 2's lower-bound paragraph only checks a few cases. I also could not rule out non-cone hosts. Partial checks on cone hosts for n=2 (8-vertex G, 9-vertex host) found no smaller example, so 3n+4 is the best-supported of the three answers, though not proven.

CHOICE: 2
